meta.title: Practical tips for working with AI tools in an Indian hospital
meta.description: Plain advice for administrators and nursing staff: what not to type into a chatbot, how to review AI output, how to read a proposal, and how to keep records.
meta.lead: These are the author’s practical suggestions, not legal requirements. Where a rule applies, the page says so and gives the section.

sections.heading: Do not paste patient information into tools you have not approved
sections.body: Names, registration numbers, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers and the contents of records should stay out of consumer chatbots. Use only tools your hospital has approved, under a written contract where patient data is involved. The DPDP Act makes the hospital responsible for personal data a vendor processes on its behalf, and allows a processor only under a valid contract (sections 8(1) and 8(2)).

sections.heading: Treat every AI draft as a draft
sections.body: Check facts, numbers and names against the source. A person who signs or sends the text is responsible for it. Decide in policy who reviews AI text before it becomes part of a patient record.

sections.heading: Keep a list of the AI tools in use
sections.body: Include the owner, what data it receives, the vendor contract, and the date of the last review. You cannot review what you cannot see, and you will need the list to answer questions about who processes patient data and to decide, tool by tool, whether the vendor treats it as a medical device.

sections.heading: Read the vendor’s answers, not the brochure
sections.body: Brochures describe capabilities. The questions in the templates page ask for status, data handling and breach notice in writing. If a question is not answered, treat it as unanswered.

sections.heading: Write the incident card before you need it
sections.body: A personal data breach has to be intimated to the Data Protection Board and to each affected person (DPDP Act, section 8(6)); the form and deadline are set in the Rules. Decide now who decides, who files, and who calls the vendor at night.

sections.heading: Offer consent and notices in the patient’s language
sections.body: The Act requires a notice and a consent request to be available in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution (sections 5(3) and 6(3)). A form only in English is a gap to close before the tool goes live.

sections.heading: Involve nursing early
sections.body: Alerts, summaries and scheduling tools change nursing work first. Ask nurse leaders what would make a tool unusable on a busy shift before you sign.
